purpose: Catch die-area inefficiencies, macro placement conflicts, and routing resource shortfalls before placement runs that take 12-48 hours consume compute and designer time. Once cells are placed, moving a 200µm×200µm macro requires re-placement of surrounding cells — a 3-5 day delay at minimum. Floorplan mistakes are the most expensive to fix late.

checks.question: Show me the utilization breakdown by voltage domain. What is the core utilization, and what does the local density look like within 10µm of every hard macro?
checks.evidence_demanded: Density heatmap at 5µm resolution from the placement tool, plus a text report of max per-region cell count. Utilization should be reported as cells/(total_area - hard_macro_area) not gross die area.
checks.red_flag: Any region within 10µm of a hard macro exceeds 85% density, or any voltage domain shows >78% core utilization. At 7nm, anything above 70% core utilization is a red flag for routing congestion.
checks.why_it_matters: Routing channels between macros need empty space for 2-3 layers of horizontal/vertical routing. High local density causes wire-length inflation, via pushout, and in extreme cases routing failures that require full re-floorplan.

checks.question: What are the aspect ratio and I/O ring width, and have you confirmed the pad pitch matches the package substrate plan?
checks.evidence_demanded: Floorplan abstract showing I/O cell placement, pad corner cell positions, and a cross-section of the die/package interface. Report of I/O cell utilization (are all power/ground pads placed?).
checks.red_flag: Aspect ratio deviates more than 15% from 1.0 without a physical-only reason (known good package). Missing power/ground pad placement causing current-density violations at package interface.
checks.why_it_matters: Package substrate routing has fixed design rules; mismatches between chip I/O ring and substrate require respin or expensive interposer rework.

checks.question: Show me the congestion map at routing layer 1-5. Where are the top 5 hotspot regions by overflow percentage?
checks.evidence_demanded: Global routing overflow report from the placement tool, with a heatmap overlay on the floorplan. Overflow % should be reported per tile, not just average.
checks.red_flag: Any tile showing >10% routing overflow at layer 1-2 before detailed routing. At 7nm, >5% overflow at M1-M2 is a red flag because those layers are used for standard cell power grid.
checks.why_it_matters: Pre-CTS global routing overflow doesn't disappear — it migrates to different layers. Hotspots at M1-M2 force detours that add 10-50ps of wire delay that timing closure won't budget for.

checks.question: Is the power grid plan complete and consistent with the IR drop analysis? Show me the max current density per strap and the estimated voltage drop at the worst corner.
checks.evidence_demanded: Power grid schematic from custom or automated grid tools, annotated with strap widths and spacing. IR drop summary report from a power grid simulation tool at max switching corner.
checks.red_flag: Estimated IR drop exceeds 5% of VDD at any standard cell cluster. At 7nm and below, >3% IR drop at the most distant standard cell from a power strap is a red flag.
checks.why_it_matters: IR drop at 7nm is not a design-for-reliability checkbox — it's a timing variable. A 30mV drop on a device with 700mV Vt margin can close timing or open it depending on sign. It must be budgeted, not guessed.

checks.question: Are all memories and specialized IPs placed with their required boundary cells and filler rings? Show me the abutment verification report.
checks.evidence_demanded: Physical abutment report from the library exchange format (LEF/DEF) verification, showing all IP boundaries, done-cell placement, and filler ring completion.
checks.red_flag: Any memory instance with missing corner cells, decoupling capacitor cells not placed per IP specification, or antenna cells not inserted at IP boundaries.
checks.why_it_matters: Memory IP has strict physical design rules around neighboring cell types. Missing boundary cells cause antenna rule violations or proximity-based leakage that only shows at tapeout physical verification — expensive to fix after routing.

checks.question: What is the pin-access feasibility at the top cell level? Show me the estimated cell access rate for the most congested 10% of standard cell rows.
checks.evidence_demanded: Pin accessibility analysis report from the place-and-route tool, with estimated access rates per row. Standard cell row utilization report.
checks.red_flag: Estimated cell access rate below 85% in any standard cell row region. At 28nm, <90% cell access in rows adjacent to large macros is a red flag.
checks.why_it_matters: Cell access failures manifest as DRC violations in detailed routing that require cell padding or placement blockages. Fixing this after placement is a 1-3 day rework cycle.

checks.question: Is the clock distribution topology sketched out at floorplan stage? Show me the conceptual CTS buffer tree placement for the top 5 highest-fanout clocks.
checks.evidence_demanded: Pre-placement clock tree synthesis preview showing estimated buffer locations, H-tree or mesh node positions, and a qualitative clock wire length estimate per clock domain.
checks.red_flag: Any clock domain with estimated wire length >5mm at 28nm or >2mm at 7nm without a mesh or trunk buffer plan.
checks.why_it_matters: Clock skew is primarily a floorplan problem solved by physical proximity. Long clock wires at floorplan stage become long clock buffers and more skew. Skew that exits floorplan review requires re-floorplanning — everything downstream is contaminated.

checks.question: At 7nm and below: have you run electromigration (EM) and self-heat analysis on the power grid? What is the projected current density vs. allowed CD for the narrowest strap?
checks.evidence_demanded: EM analysis report with current density per metal segment at max switching corner. Self-heat estimated junction temperature rise in metal segments.
checks.red_flag: Any power strap with current density above 80% of the allowed EM limit at the max-corner simulation. At 5nm, even 70% is a red flag because TDDB margins are thinner.
checks.why_it_matters: EM failures manifest as early-life field returns — chips that pass production test but fail in the field. Self-heat in narrow metal at 7nm can be 20-40°C above ambient, which reduces EM lifetime by 50% vs. room-temperature projections.

kill_questions: Show me the routing congestion map with overflow tiles highlighted. Any tile at M1-M2 exceeding 8% overflow means we re-floorplan before placement starts — we are not moving forward.

What is the IR drop at the worst-case standard cell cluster, and is it budgeted in the timing signoff library? If we have a 5% IR drop on a 700mV design without a corresponding timing margin in the liberty file, this design cannot close timing.
waiver_culture: Utilization waivers get waved at floorplan review constantly ('we'll fix density during placement'), but high-density regions that pass placement become routing detours that cost 2-4 weeks of timing closure and often end up requiring a metal-layer respin to fix the resulting DRC violations.

purpose: Catch placement quality issues, clock distribution deficiencies, and early timing violations before clock tree synthesis locks in skew and insertion delay. CTS is the most time-consuming P&R stage to fix if problems are found after it completes — a CTS rebuild at 7nm is 3-7 days of compute and designer time. This gate exists to verify placement created a solvable clock distribution problem.

checks.question: Show me the histogram of setup slack by clock group. A healthy pre-CTS review has the wall at zero — not a tail at −300ps. What percentage of paths are within 50ps of zero?
checks.evidence_demanded: Static timing analysis report from PrimeTime or Tempus, filtered by clock group, showing setup slack histogram. Path-based timing report for the worst 100 paths per clock domain.
checks.red_flag: More than 5% of paths show negative setup slack at the worst corner. Any clock group with a tail extending more than 200ps below zero at pre-CTS is a red flag because CTS will add 50-150ps of insertion delay and up to 30ps of skew.
checks.why_it_matters: Pre-CTS negative slack doesn't disappear — it gets worse. CTS adds clock insertion delay and skew to paths that are already failing setup. A design exiting pre-CTS with -200ps of worst negative slack is on track to be -500ps post-CTS without significant placement changes.

checks.question: What is the clock skew budget used in the pre-CTS timing analysis, and what does the actual skew look like across the top 10 most timing-critical clock domain crossings?
checks.evidence_demanded: Clock skew report per domain from the STA tool, showing min/max insertion delay per clock leaf. Clock domain crossing (CDC) analysis showing the skew impact on all synchronous and asynchronous boundaries.
checks.red_flag: Skew exceeding the budgeted assumption by more than 20%. Any asynchronous CDC without proper synchronization elements in the reported skew path. At 7nm, any clock domain with >20ps skew in the top 10% of paths is a red flag.
checks.why_it_matters: Clock skew is a fixed tax on timing margin. If pre-CTS analysis assumes 30ps skew and the placed design has 50ps, every setup path loses 20ps of margin. This compounds across 50,000+ critical paths and is the most common reason designs miss timing in the final STA signoff.

checks.question: Show me the estimated clock tree depth and buffer count per clock domain, and the H-tree or mesh structural integrity check.
checks.evidence_demanded: Pre-CTS clock tree estimation report showing leaf count, estimated buffer count, estimated insertion delay, and a visual of the clock trunk/mesh structure on the floorplan.
checks.red_flag: Any clock domain with estimated insertion delay more than 30% above the pre-floorplan estimate. A clock tree with more than 8 levels of buffers is a red flag at 28nm; more than 12 levels at 7nm.
checks.why_it_matters: Clock tree depth drives power and latency. Deep trees consume more clock power and add more delay per stage. If the floorplan forces a clock tree that is 2 levels deeper than estimated, that adds 100-200ps of insertion delay that may not be in the timing budget.

checks.question: Are all standard cell rows continuous? Show me the row utilization map and flag any rows with >95% cell density or discontinuous rows adjacent to hard macros.
checks.evidence_demanded: Row utilization report from the place-and-route tool, showing cell density per row. Screenshot of the floorplan with row continuity highlighted.
checks.red_flag: Any row with >95% utilization. Rows that are discontinuous (gaps in cell placement) adjacent to hard macros are a red flag because the gaps mean routing detours and longer wire paths.
checks.why_it_matters: Full rows cannot accept post-placement ECO cells. When a timing fix requires adding a buffer or sizing a cell, a 95%-full row means the fix must be placed in a distant location, adding wire length that may reintroduce the timing violation.

checks.question: What are the top 10 longest estimated wire delays for nets driving more than 4 fanouts? Show me the wire load model or spatial delay estimation for these nets.
checks.evidence_demanded: Estimated wire delay report for high-fanout nets, showing Elmore delay or RC-extracted estimates. Critical net length report, filtered for nets >500µm at 28nm or >200µm at 7nm.
checks.red_flag: Any net with estimated wire delay exceeding 200ps at 28nm or 100ps at 7nm without a repeater inserted. Any high-fanout net (>4 loads) with total wire length >2mm at 28nm or >800µm at 7nm without intermediate buffering.
checks.why_it_matters: Long high-fanout wires without repeaters become timing liabilities. Post-CTS, adding buffers to these nets requires CTS rebuild because buffers affect clock loading. Fixing long wires pre-CTS costs 1 day; post-CTS it costs 3-5 days.

checks.question: Have you verified all voltage islands and power domains are correctly isolated? Show me the level-shifter and isolation cell placement report and confirm they are not in critical timing paths.
checks.evidence_demanded: Isolation cell placement report showing all level-shifters and isolation cells. A timing path trace showing no isolation or level-shifter cell in the top 100 most critical paths.
checks.red_flag: Any isolation or level-shifter cell in the top 100 critical paths. Any power domain boundary crossing without an isolation cell where required by the power intent (CPF/UPF).
checks.why_it_matters: Isolation cells add 2-4 logic stages of delay. When they appear in critical paths at signoff, the design must either be re-floorplanned to move them out of the path or timing must be re-closed around them — both expensive at this stage.

checks.question: At 7nm and below: show me the estimated coupling capacitance as a percentage of total wire capacitance. What is the assumed aggressor spacing, and does the placement respect it?
checks.evidence_demanded: RC extraction preview report showing total coupling capacitance vs. total capacitance. Placement proximity report for parallel wires longer than 100µm.
checks.red_flag: Estimated coupling capacitance above 35% of total wire capacitance in any clock or critical signal net. Parallel wire segments >50µm with spacing below the assumed minimum at the target metal layer.
checks.why_it_matters: At 7nm, coupling capacitance can be 40-60% of total wire capacitance. If this is not accounted for in pre-CTS timing analysis, the actual delay after extraction will be 20-40% higher than estimated. This is the most common cause of pre-tapeout timing failures that require a full ECO loop.

checks.question: What is the estimated cell power consumption by clock domain, and is the power delivery network adequate at the projected switching frequency?
checks.evidence_demanded: Power estimation report per clock domain from the place-and-route tool. IR drop analysis at estimated switching activity.
checks.red_flag: Any clock domain with projected power density above the thermal design power (TDP) budget for that area. IR drop at the clock buffers exceeding the IR drop budget under estimated switching activity.
checks.why_it_matters: Clock network power is typically 30-40% of total chip power. If the placed clock tree consumes more power than budgeted, the power delivery network may not supply sufficient current at the switching corners, causing IR drop that compounds timing failures.

kill_questions: Show me the setup slack histogram by clock group. If the worst path in any clock group is more than 300ps negative at pre-CTS, we are not running CTS — we are re-placing the design. That is not negotiable at 7nm.
Is there a CDC violation in any asynchronous clock domain crossing that does not have a proper synchronizer chain? If yes, this is a functional correctness issue and the review stops here.
waiver_culture: Setup slack violations get waived at pre-CTS with the assumption that CTS will fix them through gate sizing — this is the most expensive waiver in ASIC design. CTS cannot fix -300ps of negative slack; it can only redistribute skew. Slack that exits pre-CTS negative almost always requires placement changes that cost 2-3 weeks.

purpose: Confirm timing closure is real, not a reporting artifact, before the design proceeds to mask generation. At this gate, 100% of paths must pass setup and hold analysis across all corners with sufficient margin. Mask costs at 7nm are $3-10M; a timing respin after mask generation is a project-canceling event. This gate exists to catch corner-case timing gaps, mode-dependency misses, and signoff methodology gaps that could cause a timing failure after tapeout.

checks.question: Show me the complete timing summary across all required PVT corners. How many paths fail at the worst-case corner, and what is the margin at the best corner?
checks.evidence_demanded: Timing signoff summary report from PrimeTime or Tempus covering all required corners (typically SS/0.81V/125°C, TT/0.9V/25°C, FF/0.99V/-40°C, and additional at 7nm like local variation corners). Path-based report for the worst 50 paths at each corner.
checks.red_flag: Any path with negative slack at any required signoff corner. A margin spread of more than 100ps between best and worst corner on the same clock domain is a red flag indicating incomplete correlation between corners.
checks.why_it_matters: Timing that is clean at TT but fails at SS is not closed timing. Mask generation proceeds on the assumption that timing is signoff-clean at all corners. A single failing path at SS is a mask respin risk.

checks.question: Has the signoff timing library been validated against silicon? What is the characterization gap between the library's reported delays and the measured delays on the previous process shuttle?
checks.evidence_demanded: Library characterization report with Monte Carlo variation data. If available, silicon validation data from a previous shuttle on the same process node. A written assessment of any known gap between liberty file delay models and silicon behavior.
checks.red_flag: Characterization data is more than 5% optimistic compared to silicon for any arc in the top 100 critical paths. No silicon validation data available for a 7nm or below node is a red flag that must be documented and flagged to the project lead.
checks.why_it_matters: Liberty files are models. At 7nm, modeling error of 3-5% on a 200ps critical path is 6-10ps of unaccounted error — enough to flip a path from passing to failing after silicon is fabricated.

checks.question: Show me the on-chip variation (OCV) and advanced on-chip variation (AOCV/POCV) analysis and confirm it matches the silicon characterization data. What is the derating factor applied, and is it justified?
checks.evidence_demanded: OCV/AOCV/POCV derating report from the signoff STA tool. Silicon correlation data or process characterization data supporting the derating factor. A written explanation of how the derating factor was derived.
checks.red_flag: Derating factors that are lower than what process characterization supports. At 7nm, AOCV/POCV derating below 1.05 for local variation on a 10-stage path is a red flag. No AOCV/POCV modeling — only flat OCV — is a red flag at 28nm and below.
checks.why_it_matters: OCV derating is the safety margin for within-die variation. If it's too optimistic, paths that pass signoff will fail on silicon. If it's too pessimistic, design is over-constrained and timing closure was harder than necessary. The factor must be grounded in process data, not inherited from a previous node.

checks.question: Show me the clock uncertainty budget breakdown. How much is allocated to skew, jitter, and OCV respectively, and does the total uncertainty still meet the timing budget?
checks.evidence_demanded: Clock uncertainty budget report from the STA tool, showing skew, jitter, and OCV components. A comparison of the allocated budget vs. the actual measured/skew from the built clock tree.
checks.red_flag: Clock uncertainty that exceeds the available timing budget (the difference between the clock period and the required data path delay). Any component of clock uncertainty that is larger than the margin on the worst-case path.
checks.why_it_matters: If clock uncertainty consumes 40% of the timing budget, the design is functionally correct but has no headroom for manufacturing variation. Every path must be timing-clean with the actual clock uncertainty, not an assumed value.

checks.question: Has the signoff analysis been run with actual RC extraction (not wire load models) at the target metal stack? Show me the extraction correlation report.
checks.evidence_demanded: RC extraction report from StarRC or QRC, showing total capacitance and resistance per net. A correlation report comparing wire load model estimates vs. extracted values for the critical nets.
checks.red_flag: Wire load model still used for critical paths. Extraction vs. WLM correlation error exceeding 15% on any critical net longer than 100µm. At 7nm, coupling capacitance contribution differing from assumption by more than 10%.
checks.why_it_matters: At 28nm and below, wire load models are too inaccurate for signoff. A 15% error in total capacitance on a 1ns data path is 150ps — more than the entire timing margin on most designs.

checks.question: Are all modes of operation (test mode, scan shift, at-speed test, MBIST, BIST) analyzed, and do any of them show worse timing than the functional mode?
checks.evidence_demanded: Multi-mode timing analysis report showing all operational modes. Path-based analysis for the worst path in each mode. Scan shift timing report if applicable.
checks.red_flag: Any mode with timing margins more than 20% worse than functional mode. Scan shift timing with negative hold slack is a red flag because scan chain shifts occur at a different frequency than functional operation.
checks.why_it_matters: A design that passes functional timing but fails scan timing cannot be tested at-speed, which means infant mortality screening cannot be performed. This is a functional correctness and quality issue, not just a timing issue.

checks.question: Show me the hold slack summary. A healthy design has hold slack wall at +50ps to +100ps minimum. What is the worst hold violation, and is it fixed with a buffer or is it structural?
checks.evidence_demanded: Hold slack histogram by clock group from the STA tool. Path trace for the worst 10 hold violations showing the violating cell and net.
checks.red_flag: Any negative hold slack at any corner. Positive hold slack less than 20ps at the worst corner is a concern because process variation can flip it negative. Structural hold violations (caused by placement, not by excess delay) are a red flag because ECO fixing them requires placement changes.
checks.why_it_matters: Hold violations cause functional failures — data is corrupted as it flows through the pipeline. Unlike setup violations, hold violations cannot be fixed by slowing the clock. They require adding delay (buffers) or removing delay (downsizing cells) in the data path.

checks.question: At 7nm and below: have you run path-based statistical timing (SVS/PVS) or at minimum interval timing analysis? Show me the sensitivity analysis for the top 10 critical paths to systematic variation.
checks.evidence_demanded: Statistical timing or interval timing report showing the sensitivity of critical path delay to systematic variation sources (Vth variation, channel length variation, spacer variation). A table of critical path sensitivities in ps per unit of variation.
checks.red_flag: Critical paths with sensitivity above 1.0ps/1mV of VDD variation at 7nm without a corresponding voltage margin budget. Any critical path where the sensitivity to spacer variation exceeds the available timing margin.
checks.why_it_matters: Systematic variation at 7nm is not random — it correlates spatially. A path that is marginal at nominal but sensitive to VDD droop or gate length variation will fail on silicon even if it passes corner-based signoff.

checks.question: What is the noise and crosstalk analysis result on all clock and critical data nets? Show me the delta delay report for aggressor/ victim pairs.
checks.evidence_demanded: Noise analysis report from PrimeTime noise analysis or Tempus noise analysis, showing delta delay on critical nets due to coupling. A list of aggressor/victim pairs where delta delay exceeds 10ps.
checks.red_flag: Any clock net with delta delay exceeding 5ps due to crosstalk. Any data net in the top 100 critical paths with delta delay exceeding 15ps without a noise margin budget.
checks.why_it_matters: Crosstalk-induced delay variation can add 10-30ps to a data path at 7nm. If this is not analyzed and budgeted, paths that pass signoff will fail on silicon when adjacent nets switch aggressively.

kill_questions: Show me the setup and hold slack at the SS corner for all required corners. If any path has negative slack at any signoff corner, we are not tapeout-ready. This is not a judgment call — it is a mask respin risk we cannot accept.

Has the timing library been validated against silicon at this node? If there is no silicon correlation data and this is 7nm or below, the signoff is not complete. We need a characterization gap assessment before this proceeds to tapeout.
waiver_culture: Minor timing violations (<10ps) in non-critical paths get waived as ' ECO will handle it' — but ECO slots at pre-tapeout are already consumed by functional fixes. A 5ps timing violation that becomes a 50ps violation after signoff extraction is exactly the scenario that causes tapeout respins. The culture of 'we'll ECO it' at timing signoff is responsible for more late-stage respins than any other single factor.

purpose: Confirm the layout is physically manufacturable at the target process node before mask generation. DRC (design rule check), LVS (layout vs. schematic), antenna, and ERC (electrical rule check) violations that proceed to tapeout result in zero yield — the chip will not function. This is the final correctness gate; unlike timing, a violation here cannot be ECO-fixed post-tapeout.

checks.question: Show me the DRC summary report. What are the top 5 DRC violation categories by count, and what is the total count across all categories?
checks.evidence_demanded: DRC run summary from Calibre, PVS, or ICV, showing violation count by rule, rule category, and layer. A violation density map overlaid on the floorplan for the top violation categories.
checks.red_flag: Any DRC violation of category 'short' or 'antenna'. Any DRC rule with more than 5 violations of type 'spacing' or 'width' where the violation margin is less than 10% of the rule minimum. At 7nm, any DRC at the minimum-pitch layer is a red flag.
checks.why_it_matters: DRC violations represent physical rule violations that the foundry cannot manufacture. A single short circuit means the chip has a functional electrical failure. Spacing violations at minimum-pitch layers indicate the design has no process window and will yield poorly even if it passes DRC on the reference wafer.

checks.question: Have you verified all antenna violations are resolved? Show me the antenna report and confirm the antenna ratio for the worst-case net is below the foundry limit.
checks.evidence_demanded: Antenna check report from the DRC tool showing antenna ratio per net, broken down by gate area and metal area. A list of nets with antenna ratios above 80% of the foundry limit.
checks.red_flag: Any net with an antenna ratio exceeding the foundry antenna ratio limit. Unresolved antenna violations at any metal layer above layer 3 are a red flag because they cannot be fixed with antenna diodes alone — they require layout changes.
checks.why_it_matters: Antenna violations cause gate oxide damage during manufacturing (plasma-induced charging). Chips with antenna violations pass final test but fail infant mortality screens or fail in the field. This is a reliability kill, not just a manufacturing check.

checks.question: Show me the LVS verification report. What are all open and short violations, and have you confirmed the schematic vs. layout connectivity matches for every analog and custom circuit block?
checks.evidence_demanded: LVS report from Calibre or PVS showing all open/short violations. For analog blocks, a transistor-level connectivity comparison. A confirmation that all power and ground nets match between schematic and layout.
checks.red_flag: Any open or short violation. Mismatches in analog block connectivity. Power/ground net mismatches between schematic and layout.
checks.why_it_matters: LVS opens and shorts are functional correctness failures. An open in a current mirror makes the analog block non-functional. A short between two signal nets creates an unintended logic function. LVS must be clean before tapeout — there is no waiver pathway for opens or shorts.

checks.question: What is the ERC (electrical rule check) result for ESD protection, latchup, and power-ground connectivity? Show me the ESD protection plan and confirm every I/O has a compliant ESD device.
checks.evidence_demanded: ERC report covering ESD, latchup, and power/ground connectivity checks. ESD plan document showing protection devices at every I/O. A latchup susceptibility analysis for the most sensitive analog blocks.
checks.red_flag: Any I/O without an ESD protection device. Latchup susceptibility in any I/O or analog block. Floating power or ground nodes identified by ERC. At 7nm, missing ESD devices on any GPIO is a project-stopping red flag.
checks.why_it_matters: ESD failures are field failures. A chip without adequate ESD protection fails when handled by end users. Latchup causes functional failure during normal operation when the chip is powered. Both are reliability kills that appear after the chip ships.

checks.question: Show me the density gradient analysis for all metal layers. Are all layers within the foundry-required density range, and is the gradient within the CMP plan limits?
checks.evidence_demanded: Metal density report by layer and by die region. CMP simulation output showing topography variation across the die. Density gradient report for each metal layer.
checks.red_flag: Any metal layer with density below 20% or above 80% in any 100µm×100µm window. Density gradient exceeding 30% across the die on any metal layer. At 7nm, copper density below 25% on any layer is a red flag because CMP cannot planarize low-density copper reliably.
checks.why_it_matters: Low metal density causes dishing in copper CMP; high density causes erosion. Both cause topography that breaks subsequent lithography and causes yield loss. A die that passes DRC but has CMP topography issues will have marginal yield that looks random but is actually systematic.

checks.question: At 28nm and below: have you run the foundry's signoff DRC deck, not a custom or subset deck? Show me the DRC deck version and confirm it matches the process design kit version.
checks.evidence_demanded: DRC deck manifest showing deck version, date, and foundry approval. A comparison between the deck used for verification and the foundry's official signoff deck. Confirmation that all rule checks use the foundry-provided rule deck, not a subset.
checks.red_flag: Use of a non-foundry DRC deck or a deck that is more than 6 months older than the tapeout date. Missing any rules from the foundry's mandatory signoff rule set.
checks.why_it_matters: Foundry signoff decks are the only legally binding verification standard. A design verified with a custom deck may pass those checks but fail foundry verification. The foundry will not release masks for a design that fails their verification, regardless of what a custom deck says.

checks.question: Show me the fill verification results. Are the dummy fill cells and metal fill shapes consistent with the CMP simulation, and have they been verified against the density rules?
checks.evidence_demanded: Fill verification report showing the relationship between density targets, actual fill placement, and CMP simulation output. A DRC-clean verification of the filled design (fill shapes can themselves create DRC violations).
checks.red_flag: Fill shapes creating DRC violations (spacing to active geometry, antenna effects from floating metal). Fill density that does not match the CMP simulation input — indicating the fill plan was not updated after final layout.
checks.why_it_matters: Fill shapes are metal that is electrically floating. They couple to adjacent signals and affect timing. If fill creates spacing violations or antenna issues, the design fails DRC despite having no functional cells in violation. Fill is not free of electrical consequence.

checks.question: What is the DFM (design for manufacturability) score? Show me the foundry DFM analysis results and confirm critical yield limiters have been addressed.
checks.evidence_demanded: Foundry DFM analysis report covering via redundancy, metal sliver coverage, via coverage, and critical area analysis. A written response to each DFM finding in the top 5 categories.
checks.red_flag: Critical area for random defect yield above the foundry's threshold. Via chains with less than 100% via redundancy coverage. Metal sliver coverage below 95% on critical layers.
checks.why_it_matters: DFM issues don't fail DRC — they pass verification but yield poorly. A design that is DRC-clean but has poor DFM scores may yield 60% when the target is 90%. DFM optimization is the difference between a profitable chip and a money-losing respin.

kill_questions: Show me the DRC summary. If there is a single unresolved DRC violation of category 'short' or 'open', this design does not go to tapeout. Shorts and opens are not waivable — they are functional failures.

Has the DRC been run with the foundry's official signoff deck and the current process version? If the deck is more than 6 months old or not the foundry's official deck, we re-run before this proceeds. Using an outdated deck is how designs get to the foundry and fail verification there.
waiver_culture: DRC violations in non-critical areas get waived as 'the foundry will allow it' or 'we'll do a visual inspection' — but the foundry's automated verification system does not accept visual inspections as substitutes for DRC clearance. A waived DRC violation that causes a mask failure costs $3-10M and 6-12 months of schedule. The culture of waiving DRC for 'trivial' violations is responsible for more mask respins than any other factor.
